title: GA4 & Dashboards
text:
Customer Engagement Plan Connection
My GA4 work connects to a Customer Engagement Plan focused on real estate and property-market engagement. The main goal was to understand how users move through a digital experience, where they drop off, and which traffic or device categories may be more effective for generating leads.
I used GA4 as a decision-support tool for:

Tracking homepage visits, product or property browsing, and purchase or lead actions.
Comparing web and mobile traffic in lead acquisition reports.
Using acquisition reports to identify stronger channels.
Applying funnel exploration to find conversion drop-offs.
Thinking about where BigQuery could extend GA4 analysis through deeper SQL-based work.

title: GA4 & Dashboards
text:
Reporting Focus
One of the biggest lessons I took from GA4 is that reports need to match the business question. User Acquisition and Traffic Acquisition reports are similar, but they answer different questions. User Acquisition focuses on how users first arrive, while Traffic Acquisition focuses on session-based sources.
For the Customer Engagement Plan, I selected lead acquisition by traffic type as a useful KPI. Comparing web and mobile traffic can help decide whether a marketing team should focus more on desktop experiences, mobile experiences, or both.

title: GA4 & Dashboards
text:
Funnel Exploration Summary
The funnel analysis investigated the path from homepage view to purchase:


38,514 Homepage views


335 Users moved to add to cart


124 Users continued to add payment


83 Final purchasers


The biggest issue was the early drop-off from homepage views to add-to-cart behavior. Only 335 of 38,514 homepage visitors moved forward, which showed that the homepage experience needed closer review.

title: GA4 & Dashboards
text:

Segment the funnel by traffic source and device type.
Review behavior flow to understand why users abandon the homepage.
Improve homepage product visibility and calls-to-action.
Run A/B tests on homepage layout or featured products.
Use BigQuery exports for larger trend analysis that is difficult to complete inside the GA4 interface alone.

title: R Analytics
text:
NYC Flights: Worst Arrival Delays
Identifying the 10 worst daily arrival delays across 2013, then averaging by month to reveal seasonal patterns.


Show code
library(nycflights13)

worst_delays <- flights %>%
  filter(!is.na(arr_delay)) %>%
  group_by(year, month, day) %>%
  slice_max(arr_delay, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avg_delay = mean(arr_delay))

ggplot(worst_delays, aes(x = factor(month), y = avg_delay, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2f6f73", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#c45a2d", size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Average of the 10 Worst Daily Arrival Delays by Month",
    subtitle = "NYC flights, 2013 — extreme delays are surprisingly consistent across months",
    x = "Month", y = "Average Delay (minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))









Insight: The average of the most extreme arrival delays remains relatively constant throughout the year, suggesting that factors causing very large delays (e.g., mechanical issues, air traffic control) are not strongly seasonal.

title: R Analytics
text:
Reshaping: Religion & Income Distribution
Transforming relig_income from wide to long format, then creating a grouped bar chart.


Show code
relig_long <- relig_income %>%
  pivot_longer(-religion, names_to = "income", values_to = "count") %>%
  filter(income != "Don't know/refused")

ggplot(relig_long, aes(x = religion, y = count, fill = income)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(
    title = "Income Distribution by Religious Affiliation",
    subtitle = "Reshaped from wide to long format using pivot_longer()",
    x = "Religion", y = "Number of Respondents", fill = "Income Bracket"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"

text:
Ozone vs. Temperature, Wind & Ratio


Show code
air.tib %>%
  mutate(temp_wind = Temp / Wind) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Temp, Wind, temp_wind),
               names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "#c45a2d", size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#2f6f73", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Ozone vs. Temperature, Wind, and Their Ratio",
    subtitle = "Temperature drives ozone up; wind drives it down",
    x = "Variable Value", y = "Ozone (ppb)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









Conclusion: Ozone shows a strong positive association with temperature and a negative association with wind speed. The ratio Temp/Wind does not exhibit a clear linear relationship, confirming that the individual effects are more informative.

Functional Programming in R

Reusable Chart Function
Using custom functions and lapply() to automate chart generation across multiple years.


Show code
plot_ratio <- function(year_input) {
  student_ratio %>%
    filter(year == year_input) %>%
    top_n(10, student_ratio) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(country, student_ratio), y = student_ratio)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#2f6f73", alpha = 0.85) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
      title = "Top 10 Countries by Student-Teacher Ratio",
      subtitle = paste("Year:", year_input),
      x = "", y = "Student-Teacher Ratio"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
}

title: GA4 Funnel Exploration
text:
I used the Google Analytics 4 demo account to understand how users moved through a conversion funnel from homepage view to purchase.
My purpose was to identify which stage of the journey created the greatest loss of users and then translate that finding into a practical recommendation for improving customer engagement.

title: GA4 Funnel Exploration
text:
I used the Google Analytics 4 demo account to understand how users moved through a conversion funnel from homepage view to purchase.
My purpose was to identify which stage of the journey created the greatest loss of users and then translate that finding into a practical recommendation for improving customer engagement.

title: GA4 Funnel Exploration
text:
Key Findings

38,514 homepage views began the funnel.
335 users moved to Add to Cart, a conversion rate of about 0.87%.
124 users continued to Add Payment.
83 users completed purchase.
The largest performance issue appeared at the homepage-to-add-to-cart stage.

title: GA4 Funnel Exploration
text:
Recommendation
Improve homepage product visibility and calls-to-action, then test changes through A/B experiments. The next investigation should segment funnel performance by device type and traffic source.

title: GA4 Funnel Exploration
text:
Professional Takeaway
This project helped me see how GA4 can move beyond passive reporting. The funnel gives a clear behavioral signal, and the recommendation connects directly to user experience, homepage messaging, and conversion optimization.

title: Functional Programming in R
text:
I practiced control flow, custom functions, and function mapping in R to reduce repetition and build more reusable analysis workflows.
The work connected basic programming concepts to analytics productivity. When analysis tasks repeat across years, countries, groups, or variables, functions make the work easier to scale and easier to check.

Functional programming also supports Quarto reporting because reusable functions can power repeated charts, parameterized reports, and automated summaries.
